mainTopic: Responsibility for damage in someone else's courtyard: how permission, guarding and intruding decide who pays.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a question from the previous amud: does a בעל חצר who gives permission to bring things into his courtyard take responsibility for them? Two ברייתות that seemed to prove this are explained as talking about the owner of the damaging ox instead. For the eating case, permission decides whether it counts as שן in the victim's domain or in the public domain. For the goring case, the ברייתא follows רבי טרפון, and permission decides between full and half damage. Next, רבא makes a woman who came in to bake pay for the homeowner's goat that died from eating her dough. The גמרא shows this fits with רב: she came with permission, and because baking needs privacy, the owners leave and the guarding falls on her. The amud then brings several rulings of רבא about entering a courtyard without permission: an ox that digs pits, an ox that injures the homeowner or drops dung (which counts as a בור), and a person who intrudes. רב פפא adds that a homeowner who knows the intruder is there may throw him out but may not hurt him. The amud ends by introducing another statement of רבא or רב פפא, which is quoted on the next amud.

steps.title: What difference does permission make for the ox's owner?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the reading that the earlier ברייתא about produce is talking about the ox's owner. If so, why would it matter whether the produce was brought in with permission?
steps.simpleTranslation: What difference is there between 'with permission' and 'without permission'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is continuing from just before this section. It had said the ברייתא about produce eaten by a stranger's ox is talking about the ox's owner, and now it asks why permission would matter for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner of the ox has nothing to do with the deal between the produce owner and the בעל חצר. So it seems that whether the courtyard owner gave permission should not change whether the ox's owner pays. This puts pressure on the reading that the ברייתא is about the ox's owner.

phrases.english: What is there in 'with permission'
and what is there in 'without permission'?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי בִּרְשׁוּת וּמַאי שֶׁלֹּא בִּרְשׁוּת אִיכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading, given just before this section, that the produce ברייתא is about the ox's owner.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that 'exempt' and 'liable' in the produce ברייתא refer to the ox's owner.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ox's owner is a stranger to the permission arrangement, so permission should not affect whether he pays.

steps.title: Permission decides whose domain the courtyard counts as
steps.stepSummary: The answer: with permission, the courtyard counts as the produce owner's domain, so it is שן in the victim's domain, and the ox's owner pays. Without permission, it counts like the public domain, and שן there is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: With permission, it is a case of שן in the injured party's domain, and שן in the injured party's domain is liable. Without permission, it is a case of שן in the public domain, and שן in the public domain is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question and shows that permission really does matter, even for the ox's owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Permission changes the status of the place where the damage happened. When the produce is there with permission, the place counts as the owner's own domain, and eating there makes the ox's owner liable. Without permission the produce is not in its owner's domain, and eating there is treated like eating in the public domain, which is exempt. So the ברייתא is fully explained without saying anything about the בעל חצר taking responsibility.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Tooth' – the category of damage where an animal eats for its own benefit
The domain of the injured party

steps.whyThisMatters: It uses a basic rule from the start of the מסכתא: שן pays only in the victim's domain, not in the public domain.

phrases.english: They said: With permission –
it is a case of Eating in the domain of the injured party,
phrases.notes: Because he has permission, the spot where his produce sits counts as his own place.

phrases.english: and Eating in the domain of the injured party is liable.
Without permission –
it is a case of Eating in the public domain,
and Eating in the public domain is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: בִּרְשׁוּת הָוְיָא לַהּ שֵׁן בִּרְשׁוּת הַנִּיזָּק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the location: permission decides whether the place counts as the victim's domain or as the public domain.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Permission seemed to matter only between the produce owner and the בעל חצר, not to the ox's owner.
steps.terutzMaskana: Permission decides whether the case falls under liable שן (victim's domain) or exempt שן (public domain), so the ברייתא proves nothing about the בעל חצר.

steps.title: New proof: an ox gored inside the courtyard
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא. Someone's ox is gored inside another person's courtyard: without permission, 'exempt'; with permission, 'liable'. It suggests that this means the בעל חצר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If someone brought his ox into a homeowner's courtyard without permission, and an ox from elsewhere came and gored it, he is exempt. If he brought it in with permission, he is liable. Who is exempt and who is liable? Is it not the בעל חצר who is exempt and the בעל חצר who is liable?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a fresh source to prove that a courtyard owner who gives permission takes on responsibility for what is brought in.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the damage is goring (קרן), and the owner of a goring ox pays no matter where it happens. So permission seems irrelevant for the goring ox's owner. That suggests the person who is 'liable with permission' must be the בעל חצר, who took on responsibility by agreeing.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear – introduces a proof
Is it not…? (introduces a suggested reading)

phrases.english: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: הִכְנִיס שׁוֹרוֹ לַחֲצַר בַּעַל הַבַּיִת שֶׁלֹּא בִּרְשׁוּת,
phrases.english: If one brought his ox into a homeowner's courtyard without permission,

phrases.aramaic: וּבָא שׁוֹר מִמָּקוֹם אַחֵר וּנְגָחוֹ – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: and an ox from elsewhere came and gored it – exempt.
But if he brought it in with permission – liable.
Who is exempt and who is liable?
Is it not the owner of the courtyard who is exempt,
and the owner of the courtyard who is liable?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הִכְנִיס שׁוֹרוֹ לַחֲצַר בַּעַל הַבַּיִת שֶׁלֹּא בִּרְשׁוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the produce ברייתא was explained away, a new ברייתא is brought for the same question.
steps.raayaObject: That a courtyard owner who gives permission accepts responsibility for what is brought in.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about an ox gored in a homeowner's courtyard, read as referring to the בעל חצר.

steps.title: No, it is talking about the goring ox's owner
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes off the proof. 'Exempt' and 'liable' may refer to the owner of the ox that gored, not to the בעל חצר.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. The owner of the ox is exempt, and the owner of the ox is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof by reading the ברייתא as being about the owner of the goring ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ברייתא is about the goring ox's owner, it says nothing about whether the בעל חצר took on responsibility. This is the same move the גמרא used with the produce ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: The owner of the ox (here, the one that gored)

phrases.english: No; the owner of the ox is exempt,
and the owner of the ox is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא; פָּטוּר בַּעַל הַשּׁוֹר, וְחַיָּיב בַּעַל הַשּׁוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 3.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the identification of who pays. It does not reject the ruling in the ברייתא.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the unnamed party had to be the בעל חצר, but it could be the goring ox's owner.

steps.title: Then why would permission matter for goring?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the rejection. If the ברייתא is about the goring ox's owner, permission should make no difference, because goring is liable everywhere.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, what difference is there between 'with permission' and 'without permission'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats its earlier question, but now about goring. This time the answer from step 2 does not seem to work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With שן, permission mattered because שן is exempt in the public domain. קרן is different: the owner of a goring ox pays even in the public domain. So if the ברייתא is about the goring ox's owner, the line between with and without permission seems pointless, and the rejection looks weak.

keyTerms.meaning: If so – introduces a challenge to what was just said

steps.confusionAlert: Same words as step 1, but a different case. In step 1 the damage was eating (שן), which depends on location. Here it is goring (קרן), which is liable everywhere, so the step 2 answer does not carry over.
steps.whatToRemember: The produce ברייתא was explained through the location rule of שן. That rule does not work for goring, so the reading that the goring ברייתא is about the goring ox's owner needs a new explanation. The next step gives it.

phrases.english: If so, what is there in 'with permission'
phrases.notes: A goring ox's owner pays even in the public domain, so the location trick from before does not help here.

phrases.english: and what is there in 'without permission'?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, מַאי בִּרְשׁוּת וּמַאי שֶׁלֹּא בִּרְשׁוּת אִיכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rejection in step 4 by repeating the step 1 question in a case where the step 2 answer does not apply.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the goring ברייתא is about the owner of the goring ox.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: קרן is liable even in the public domain, so permission cannot change the goring ox owner's liability. The ברייתא's distinction would then be meaningless.

steps.title: The ברייתא follows רבי טרפון: permission decides between full and half damage
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is about the goring ox's owner, and it follows רבי טרפון. With permission it is קרן in the victim's courtyard, so he pays full damage. Without permission it is like קרן in the public domain, so he pays only half.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answered: This ברייתא follows רבי טרפון, who says goring in the injured person's courtyard is different, and the owner pays full damage. So with permission, it is goring in the injured person's courtyard, and he pays full damage. Without permission, it is goring in the public domain, and he pays only half damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 5. It shows that permission does matter for goring if we follow רבי טרפון's opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 assumed goring is treated the same everywhere, so permission should not matter. רבי טרפון holds that קרן in the victim's own courtyard pays full damage instead of half, so where the goring happened now changes the payment. Permission decides whether the courtyard counts as the victim's place (full) or like the public domain (half).

keyTerms.meaning: Whose opinion is this? (asking which תנא the source follows)
Is different, has a special rule
Goring in the injured party's own courtyard
Half payment for the damage (the usual rule for a first-time gorer)

steps.confusionAlert: Here the ברייתא's 'exempt' does not mean he pays nothing. It means he is exempt from the extra half, so he pays only חצי נזק. 'Liable' means he pays נזק שלם.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא about an ox gored in someone else's courtyard follows רבי טרפון. Permission decides whether the goring ox's owner pays full damage or half.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרִי: הָא מַנִּי – רַבִּי טַרְפוֹן הִיא,
phrases.english: They said: Whose opinion is this? It is Rabbi Tarfon's,
who says: Goring in the injured party's courtyard is different,
he pays full damage.
phrases.notes: A first-time gorer normally pays only half. רבי טרפון says that in the victim's own courtyard he pays the whole amount.

phrases.aramaic: בִּרְשׁוּת – הָוְיָא לַהּ קֶרֶן בַּחֲצַר הַנִּיזָּק,
phrases.english: With permission, it is goring in the injured party's courtyard,
and he pays full damage;

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא בִּרְשׁוּת – הָוְיָא לַהּ קֶרֶן בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים,
phrases.english: without permission, it is goring in the public domain,
and he pays only half damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: הָא מַנִּי – רַבִּי טַרְפוֹן הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 5's challenge and so supports step 4's rereading of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the ברייתא to a specific תנא (רבי טרפון) whose view makes the distinction meaningful
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Goring is liable everywhere, so permission should make no difference to the goring ox's owner.
steps.terutzMaskana: According to רבי טרפון, קרן in the victim's courtyard pays full damage. Permission therefore decides between full and half payment.
steps.whyThisMatters: This closes the attempted proof from step 3. The ברייתא can be explained as talking about the goring ox's owner, so it does not prove anything about the בעל חצר.

steps.title: A woman's dough kills the homeowner's goat, and רבא makes her pay
steps.stepSummary: A woman came into a house to bake. The homeowner's goat ate her dough, overheated and died. רבא ruled that she must pay for the goat.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain woman went into a certain house to bake. A goat belonging to the owner of the house came and ate the dough, became overheated and died. רבא made her pay the value of the goat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real case and gives רבא's ruling. This sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the damage goes the other way: the visitor's property (the dough) harmed the homeowner's animal. רבא held the visitor responsible even though the goat came and ate on its own.

phrases.english: A certain woman who entered
to bake in a certain house,
a goat of the owner of the house came
and ate the dough, became overheated and died.
Rava obligated her to pay the value of the goat.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַהִיא אִיתְּתָא דְּעַלַּא לְמֵיפָא בְּהָהוּא בֵּיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: a story and ruling about a visitor's property harming the homeowner's animal.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A woman who came in to bake must pay when the homeowner's goat eats her dough and dies.

steps.title: Does רבא disagree with רב's rule that the animal should not have eaten?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רבא's ruling argues with רב. רב said that if an animal eats someone's produce and dies, the produce owner is exempt, because the animal should not have eaten.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say רבא disagrees with רב? For רב said: The animal should not have eaten it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's ruling by placing it next to רב's ruling, which seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב exempted the produce owner when the homeowner's animal ate his produce and died, since the animal should not have eaten. רבא made the woman pay in what looks like the same situation. So it seems they disagree.

keyTerms.meaning: It should not have eaten (so the owner of the food is not responsible)

phrases.english: Shall we say this disagrees with Rav?

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב: הֲוָיא לַהּ שֶׁלֹּא תֹּאכַל?
phrases.english: For Rav said: It should not have eaten.
phrases.notes: This points back to רב's ruling on the previous amud: produce brought into a courtyard without permission, which the homeowner's animal ate and died from.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא פְּלִיגָא אַדְּרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's ruling in step 7 using רב's earlier ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that the woman pays for the goat
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב exempts the food owner because the animal should not have eaten, and רבא makes the food owner pay. That looks like a direct disagreement.

steps.title: Permission means accepting responsibility to guard
steps.stepSummary: The cases differ. In רב's case the produce came in without permission, so its owner never took on responsibility to guard. Here the woman came in with permission, so she did take on responsibility to guard.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answered: How can you compare? There, it was without permission, so he did not accept responsibility to guard. Here, it was with permission, so she accepted responsibility to guard.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing that רב and רבא are talking about different cases, so they do not disagree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key difference is permission. Coming in with permission means the guest takes on the duty to watch her things so they do not cause damage, so she pays. Without permission no such duty was taken on, and רב's reason 'it should not have eaten' applies.

keyTerms.meaning: How can you compare? (the cases are not alike)
Accepted upon himself, took on responsibility

steps.whatToRemember: Someone who brings things into another person's home with permission takes on responsibility to guard them, so he pays if they harm the homeowner's animal. Without permission, the animal 'should not have eaten,' and he is exempt.

phrases.english: They said: How can you compare?!
There, it was without permission,
so he did not accept responsibility for guarding;
here, it was with permission,
so she accepted responsibility for guarding.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: הָכִי הַשְׁתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 8 by showing that רב's case and רבא's case are different.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (permission versus no permission)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא and רב disagree about whether the food owner pays when an animal eats the food and dies.
steps.terutzMaskana: No disagreement: with permission the guest accepts guarding and pays, and without permission there was no guarding duty, so he is exempt.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets a clear practical principle: entering with permission brings a duty to guard one's belongings so they do not harm the host.

steps.title: The woman who came in to grind wheat
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges Step 9 using a ברייתא. A woman who came in to grind wheat without permission is liable if the homeowner's animal is hurt by her wheat. That implies she would be exempt if she came with permission, which seems to contradict רבא's ruling about the baking woman.
steps.simpleTranslation: How is this different from the ברייתא about a woman who came into a homeowner's place without permission to grind wheat? There, if the homeowner's animal ate the wheat, he is exempt, and if the animal was hurt, she is liable. The reason she is liable is that she came without permission. So if she came with permission, she would be exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from Step 9 by bringing a ברייתא that seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 9 said that coming in with permission means you take on the duty to guard. But this ברייתא makes the woman liable only because she came without permission. That implies that with permission she is exempt, so permission did not make her responsible for guarding.

keyTerms.meaning: And how is it different? (introduces a contradiction)

phrases.english: And how is it different from the woman
who came in to grind wheat
at a homeowner's place without permission

phrases.aramaic: וַאֲכָלָתַן בְּהֶמְתּוֹ שֶׁל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת – פָּטוּר
phrases.english: and the homeowner's animal ate them: he is exempt
and if it was hurt: she is liable
The reason is that it was without permission
but with permission, she would be exempt!
phrases.notes: The ה in square brackets is the corrected wording, so read it as 'she is exempt.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאי שְׁנָא מֵהָאִשָּׁה שֶׁנִּכְנְסָה לִטְחוֹן חִטִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the distinction made in Step 9
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 9's claim that entering with permission means taking on the duty to guard
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The grinding woman is liable only because she came without permission, which implies that permission alone does not create a duty to guard.

steps.title: Grinding needs no privacy, but baking does
steps.stepSummary: Grinding needs no privacy, so the homeowners stay in the courtyard and the guarding stays their job. Baking needs privacy, so the homeowners leave and the guarding becomes her job.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answered: when she comes to grind wheat, she needs no privacy at all. So the owners of the courtyard do not leave, and the guarding stays their job. But when she comes to bake, she needs privacy. So the owners of the courtyard leave, and therefore the guarding becomes her job.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by pointing to a real difference between grinding and baking.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Permission by itself does not move the guarding duty. What matters is who is actually there to watch. When the owners leave so the baker can have privacy, she is the only one present, so the guarding falls on her.

keyTerms.meaning: they take themselves away, they leave

steps.whatToRemember: The guarding duty follows whoever is actually present. When the homeowners stay, the job is theirs. When they leave for the guest's privacy, the job is the guest's.

phrases.english: They said: to grind wheat
since she does not need any privacy at all
the owners of the courtyard do not take themselves away
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets, 'need'; the meaning stays the same.

phrases.english: and the guarding falls on him
phrases.notes: "Him" here means the homeowner, who stays nearby.

phrases.english: But to bake
since she needs privacy
the owners of the courtyard take themselves away
therefore the guarding falls on her.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: לִטְחוֹן חִטִּים, כֵּיוָן דְּלָא בָּעֲיָא צְנִיעוּתָא מִידֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 10
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Permission works the same way in both cases, so the baking woman should be exempt like the grinding woman.
steps.terutzMaskana: Baking needs privacy, so the owners leave and she must guard. Grinding does not, so the owners stay and keep the guarding duty.

steps.title: An ox that digs pits in another person's courtyard
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא moves to the next line of the משנה. רבא rules that if one brings his ox into a courtyard without permission and it digs pits, the ox owner pays for the damage to the courtyard. The courtyard owner is liable for damage caused by the pit.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'If he brought his ox into the homeowner's courtyard.' רבא said: if a person brought his ox into a homeowner's courtyard without permission, and it dug pits, ditches and caves there, the ox owner is liable for the damage to the courtyard. The courtyard owner is liable for the damage caused by the pit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next phrase of the משנה and brings a new ruling from רבא about an ox that digs pits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two separate damages here. Digging up the courtyard is damage the ox did, so the ox owner pays. But once the pit is in the courtyard owner's property, he is the one responsible if someone later falls in.

keyTerms.meaning: damage caused by the pit (to whoever falls in)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two payments. The ox owner pays for ruining the courtyard. The courtyard owner pays only for what later falls into the pit.

phrases.english: "If he brought his ox into the homeowner's courtyard."
Rava said:

phrases.aramaic: הִכְנִיס שׁוֹרוֹ לַחֲצַר בַּעַל הַבַּיִת שֶׁלֹּא בִּרְשׁוּת
phrases.english: If one brought his ox into a homeowner's courtyard without permission
and it dug pits, ditches and caves in it
the ox owner is liable for the damage to the courtyard
and the courtyard owner is liable for the damage caused by the pit.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִכְנִיס שׁוֹרוֹ לַחֲצַר בַּעַל הַבַּיִת. אָמַר רָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic based on the next line of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ox owner pays for the damage to the courtyard. The courtyard owner is liable for damage caused by the pit.

steps.title: Why the courtyard owner is liable for a pit his ox did not dig
steps.stepSummary: There is a rule that a pit dug by an ox brings no pit liability. Even so, the courtyard owner should have filled in this pit and did not, so he counts as if he dug it himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even though the Master said that the פסוק 'When a man digs a pit' teaches that a man brings liability for a pit, but an ox does not, here it is different. Since the courtyard owner should have filled the pit and did not fill it, he is considered like the one who dug it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains רבא's ruling by answering an obvious question before anyone asks it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually a pit dug by an ox brings no pit liability, because the פסוק says 'a man.' But the courtyard owner had the chance to fill it in and left it open. Leaving it open makes him count as the digger.

keyTerms.meaning: when a man digs a pit (the פסוק)
he is like the one who dug it

steps.whatToRemember: An owner who could fill a dangerous pit on his property and leaves it open is treated as if he dug it himself.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that liability for a pit can come from leaving a danger in place, not only from making it.

phrases.english: Even though the Master said:

phrases.aramaic: ״כִּי יִכְרֶה אִישׁ בּוֹר״ – וְלֹא שׁוֹר בּוֹר;
phrases.english: "When a man digs a pit": and not an ox that digs a pit

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא, כֵּיוָן דְּאִית לֵיהּ לְהַאיְךְ לְמַלּוֹיֵיהּ
phrases.english: here, since that one should have filled it
and he did not fill it
he is considered like the one who dug it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף עַל גַּב דְּאָמַר מָר: כִּי יִכְרֶה אִישׁ בּוֹר וְלֹא שׁוֹר בּוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers an unasked question about רבא's ruling in Step 12
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing who counts as the digger
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A pit dug by an ox brings no pit liability, so the courtyard owner should be exempt.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because he should have filled the pit and did not, the courtyard owner counts as the one who dug it.

steps.title: רבא's ruling on an ox brought in without permission
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that one who brings his ox into a courtyard without permission is liable if the ox injures the homeowner or the homeowner is hurt by it. If the ox 'crouched', he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא said: If someone brought his ox into a homeowner's courtyard without permission, and it injured the homeowner, or the homeowner was hurt by it, the ox's owner is liable. If it 'crouched', he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ruling of רבא about an ox that was brought into someone else's courtyard without permission.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the ox came in without permission, its owner is responsible for the harm it does to the homeowner. The surprising part is the last line: if the ox 'crouched', the owner is exempt. That puzzling ending sets up the next question.

keyTerms.meaning: The homeowner's courtyard (someone else's private property)
Was injured by it (the homeowner tripped over the ox)

phrases.english: And רבא said:
If one brought his ox into a homeowner's courtyard
without permission,
and it injured the homeowner,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ בַּעַל הַבַּיִת הוּזַּק בּוֹ – חַיָּיב.
phrases.english: or the homeowner was injured by it, he is liable.
If it crouched, he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another ruling of רבא, like the one in Step 12, about an ox brought into a courtyard without permission.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An ox brought in without permission makes its owner liable for injuring the homeowner or for the homeowner being hurt by it. If it 'רבץ', the owner is exempt.

steps.title: Why should crouching make him exempt?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא is puzzled. Why would the ox's owner be exempt just because the ox crouched?
steps.simpleTranslation: And just because it crouched, he is exempt?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the last line of רבא's ruling. Why should crouching be any different from other harm the ox causes?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ox came in without permission, so its owner should be responsible for everything it does. Lying down and crushing something is normal animal behavior, so there seems to be no reason to exempt him. The question pushes us to find what 'רבץ' really means here.

keyTerms.meaning: Said with surprise: 'Just because it crouched, he's exempt?!'

phrases.english: And because it crouched, he is exempt?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִשּׁוּם דְּרָבַץ, פָּטוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the exemption at the end of רבא's ruling in Step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The exemption 'רבץ – פטור' in רבא's ruling.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An ox brought in without permission makes its owner responsible for its actions. Crouching is ordinary animal behavior, so there is no clear reason it should bring an exemption.

steps.title: רב פפא: it means the ox dropped dung
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that 'רבץ' means the ox dropped dung that dirtied the homeowner's things. Dung counts as a בור, and a בור never makes one pay for damaged objects.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: What does 'רבץ' mean? That it dropped dung, and the homeowner's things got dirty. The dung counts as a pit, and we never find that a pit makes someone liable for damaged objects.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers the question by explaining that 'רבץ' here does not mean crouching. It means the ox dropped dung.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once we read 'רבץ' as dropping dung, the damage falls into the category of בור, an obstacle left lying where things can be hurt. בור pays for harm to living beings but never for harm to כלים. That is why the ox's owner is exempt when the homeowner's things get dirty.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who explains רבא's words
Pit; the damage category for obstacles left lying around
We have not found (no such rule exists)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'רבץ' here as 'crouched'. רב פפא explains it as a play on the word: 'הרבּיץ' means it dropped dung.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the ox's owner is exempt here because of the rule that בור does not pay for objects. It has nothing to do with whether the ox came in with permission.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
What is 'crouched'? That it dropped dung,
and the homeowner's belongings got dirty;
for the dung counts as a pit,
and we have not found a pit
for which one is made liable for objects.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: מַאי ״רָבַץ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 15 by explaining the word 'רבץ' differently.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining a word differently (crouched becomes dropped dung), which moves the case into the category of בור.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'רבץ' means the ox crouched, so there seemed to be no reason for an exemption.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'רבץ' means it dropped dung. Dung is a בור, and a בור never pays for damaged objects, so the owner is exempt.

steps.title: This works for שמואל, but what about רב?
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא's answer works for שמואל, who holds that any obstacle counts as a בור. But רב holds that an obstacle counts as a בור only once its owner gives up ownership. How would רב explain the exemption?
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for שמואל, who said any obstacle counts as a pit. But according to רב, who said it isn't a pit until the owner gives up ownership of it, what can we say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב פפא's answer. It points out that the answer seems to depend on one side of a known argument between רב and שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For שמואל, the dung is automatically a בור, so the rule exempting objects applies. For רב, something left lying around becomes a בור only if the owner gave it up. Until then it is still treated as his own damaging property, and the exemption for objects would not apply. So how can רבא's exemption work according to רב?

keyTerms.meaning: It works out well (according to one view)
An אמורא who holds that any obstacle is a בור
An obstacle someone could trip over or be harmed by
An אמורא who holds that an obstacle is a בור only once it is given up
What is there to say? (a challenge formula)

phrases.english: This works well for Shmuel, who said:
Any obstacle is a pit.
But according to Rav, who said:
[it is not a pit] until he gives up ownership of it,
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets aren't written in the גמרא, but they are understood from the line before.

phrases.english: what is there to say?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנִיחָא לִשְׁמוּאֵל, דְּאָמַר: כׇּל תַּקָּלָה – בּוֹר הוּא. אֶלָּא לְרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב פפא's answer from Step 16 using the argument between רב and שמואל.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's claim that the dung counts as a בור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: According to רב, an obstacle counts as a בור only once its owner gives it up. Unless the dung was given up, it would not be a בור, and the exemption for objects would not apply.

steps.title: People normally give up ordinary dung
steps.stepSummary: The answer: people normally give up ownership of ordinary dung, so it counts as a בור even according to רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: Ordinary dung, a person gives up ownership of it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It explains that dung is something people normally give up, so רב would also call it a בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב requires the owner to give up the obstacle before it counts as a בור. Nobody wants ordinary dung, so we assume the owner gave it up without saying so. That makes the dung a בור for רב too, and רבא's exemption for the dirtied objects works for everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: He surely gives up ownership of them

steps.whatToRemember: רבא exempts the ox's owner when 'רבץ' because it means the ox dropped dung. Dung is a בור, and a בור never pays for objects. This works for both שמואל and רב, because people normally give up ownership of ordinary dung.

phrases.english: They said:
Ordinary dung, he certainly gives up ownership of it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי: סְתָם גְּלָלִים – אַפְקוֹרֵי מַפְקַיר לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 17 by showing that dung meets רב's requirement.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining the normal case: ordinary dung is assumed to be given up, so it meets רב's condition.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: According to רב, the dung would not be a בור unless the owner clearly gave it up, so the exemption seemed to fail.
steps.terutzMaskana: People normally give up ownership of dung, so it is a בור even for רב, and the exemption for objects applies.

steps.title: רבא's rule for a person who enters a courtyard without permission
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that one who enters a courtyard without permission is liable for injuries to the homeowner, and the homeowner is exempt if he injures the intruder.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא said: If someone entered a homeowner's courtyard without permission, and he injured the homeowner, or the homeowner was hurt by bumping into him, the intruder is liable. If the homeowner injured him, the homeowner is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another ruling from רבא. This one is about an uninvited person in someone else's courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier ruling was about an ox brought in without permission. Now רבא applies the same idea to a person. Because the intruder had no right to be there, he pays for any harm, and the homeowner does not pay if he hurts him.

keyTerms.meaning: The homeowner, the owner of the courtyard
Was injured by him, for example by tripping over him

steps.confusionAlert: There are two different people who can get hurt here. If the homeowner is hurt, the intruder pays. If the intruder is hurt by the homeowner, the homeowner is exempt. Keep track of who is hurting whom.

phrases.english: And Rava said:
If one entered the courtyard of a homeowner
without permission,
and he injured the homeowner
or the homeowner was injured by him,
he is liable.
If the homeowner injured him, he is exempt.
phrases.notes: Here the one who is exempt is the homeowner.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second ruling of רבא, parallel to his ox ruling in step 14, now about a person.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An intruder without permission pays for injuries to the homeowner; the homeowner is exempt for injuring the intruder.

steps.title: רב פפא limits the homeowner's exemption
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says the homeowner is exempt only if he did not know the intruder was there. If he knew, he is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: We only said the homeowner is exempt when he did not know the intruder was there. But if he knew, and the homeowner injured him, the homeowner is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא adds a limit to the last part of רבא's rule, the part where the homeowner is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's exemption for the homeowner is not total. It depends on whether the homeowner knew someone was in his courtyard. If he knew, he pays, because (as the next step explains) his right to throw the intruder out is not a right to injure him.

keyTerms.meaning: We only said this when, a phrase that limits an earlier rule
Knew about him, was aware he was there

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: We said this
only where he did not know about him;
phrases.notes: "He" is the homeowner, and "him" is the intruder.

phrases.english: but if he knew about him,
if the homeowner injured him, he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: לָא אֲמַרַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the homeowner's exemption in רבא's ruling to a case where he did not know the intruder was there.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The homeowner is exempt for injuring an intruder only if he did not know the intruder was there; if he knew, he is liable.

steps.title: Why the homeowner pays if he knew
steps.stepSummary: The reason is that a right to throw someone out is not a right to hurt him.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? Because the intruder can say to him: Granted, you have the right to throw me out, but you do not have the right to injure me.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רב פפא makes the homeowner pay, and gives the reason right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The intruder admits he had no right to be there. But that only lets the homeowner remove him. It does not let the homeowner harm him once he knows he is there.
steps.whatToRemember: An intruder can be thrown out, but a homeowner who knows he is there may not hurt him. If he does, the homeowner pays.

phrases.english: What is the reason? Because he can say to him:
phrases.notes: The injured intruder is speaking to the homeowner.

phrases.english: Granted that you have the right to throw me out,
you do not have the right to injure me.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for רב פפא's limit in step 20.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is the homeowner liable when he knew the intruder was there?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The right to remove an intruder does not include a right to injure him.

steps.title: רבא and רב פפא follow their own reasoning
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that רבא and רב פפא are consistent with another statement of theirs, which it is about to quote.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they follow their own reasoning, as רבא said, and some say it was רב פפא:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא says these rulings match another statement of רבא (or רב פפא), and is about to quote it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא wants to show that the idea behind these rulings, that one who enters without permission is responsible, also shows up in another ruling. The actual statement is quoted on the next amud. There is a doubt whether it was said by רבא or by רב פפא.

keyTerms.meaning: They follow their own reasoning, they are consistent with their other views
And some say, it is also reported in the name of

phrases.english: And they follow their own reasoning,
phrases.notes: "They" means רבא and רב פפא, whose rulings we just learned.

phrases.english: as Rava said, and some say it was Rav Pappa:

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָזְדוּ לְטַעְמַיְיהוּ, דְּאָמַר רָבָא וְאִיתֵּימָא רַב פָּפָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Links the rulings of steps 19-21 to another statement of the same אמוראים, which is about to be quoted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The rulings of רבא and רב פפא match another statement of theirs, introduced here.
